questions.stem: Which statement about electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum is correct?
options: Radio waves travel at c, but X-rays travel much faster than c
Its speed depends on how bright the source of the radiation is
All of it travels at the same speed, c, whatever its frequency
Higher-frequency radiation travels faster than lower-frequency radiation
questions.explanation: Radio waves, visible light, X-rays and every other part of the spectrum travel at c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength, linked by c = fλ, not in speed.

questions.stem: What must an electric charge be doing for it to emit electromagnetic waves?
options: Accelerating, for example oscillating back and forth in an antenna
Moving at a steady, constant velocity along a straight wire
Sitting stationary while held at a high electric potential
Vibrating the air molecules around it, as a sound source does
questions.explanation: An accelerating charge, for example one oscillating back and forth in an antenna, produces changing electric and magnetic fields that travel outward as an electromagnetic wave. A charge at rest or moving at constant velocity does not radiate. Sound, not light, is a vibration of particles in a medium.

questions.stem: Which description of a travelling electromagnetic wave is correct?
options: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields that need a medium to carry them
Electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
Electric and magnetic fields oscillating parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
An oscillating electric field only, perpendicular to the direction of travel
questions.explanation: In an electromagnetic wave, a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field and vice versa, so the wave sustains itself without a medium. The two fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, making the wave transverse.

questions.stem: Maxwell predicted the speed of electromagnetic waves using c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). With ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ N A⁻², what value does this give?
options: 9.0 × 10¹⁶ m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: ε₀μ₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁷, and 1/√(1.11 × 10⁻¹⁷) ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 9.0 × 10¹⁶, and forgetting to take the reciprocal leaves 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁷.

questions.stem: Why was Maxwell's calculation of c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀) so significant?
options: It showed that electric and magnetic fields cannot exist in a vacuum
It matched the measured speed of light, so light is an electromagnetic wave
It showed that light travels faster in glass than it does through a vacuum
It proved that light is made of particles carrying an electric charge
questions.explanation: The constants ε₀ and μ₀ come from measurements of electric and magnetic forces, yet the speed they give agreed closely with the measured speed of light. Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. Light travels more slowly in glass than in a vacuum.

questions.stem: In Hertz's experiments, what did the spark-gap oscillator and the loop antenna do?
options: The oscillator measured the charge on an electron, and the loop measured its mass
The oscillator emitted electromagnetic waves, and sparks across the loop's gap detected them
The oscillator detected light from the Sun, and the loop converted it into a steady current
The oscillator produced sound waves, and the loop measured their frequency by resonance
questions.explanation: Sparks across the oscillator's gap made charges surge back and forth, radiating electromagnetic waves. A loop of wire with a small gap, some distance away, showed sparks when the waves reached it, showing that energy had travelled through space as Maxwell predicted.

questions.stem: How did Hertz verify the predicted speed of the waves from his oscillator?
options: He found the wavelength from standing waves, and with the known frequency calculated v = fλ ≈ c
He timed a single pulse over several kilometres with a stopwatch and divided distance by time
He measured the brightness of the sparks at different distances and used the inverse square law
He compared the colour of the sparks with sunlight and found the two had the same wavelength
questions.explanation: Hertz reflected the waves from a metal sheet to set up standing waves and used his detector to locate the nodes, which are half a wavelength apart. Combining that wavelength with the frequency of his oscillator gave a speed close to the speed of light. He also showed that the waves could be reflected, refracted and polarised like light.

questions.stem: Students remove the turntable from a microwave oven (2.45 GHz) and heat a slab of chocolate. Melted spots form 6.0 cm apart, half a wavelength. What speed of light does this give, and what is the percentage error from 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹?
options: 1.47 × 10¹¹ m s⁻¹, an error of 49%
2.94 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, an error of 2.0%
1.47 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, an error of 51%
2.94 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, an error of 0.6%
questions.explanation: The wavelength is 2 × 6.0 = 12.0 cm, so v = fλ = 2.45 × 10⁹ × 0.120 = 2.94 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The percentage error is (3.00 − 2.94)/3.00 × 100 = 2.0%. Using 6.0 cm as the full wavelength gives half the speed.

questions.stem: A class measures the speed of light and gets a mean of 3.12 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, with all results close together. Which statement best assesses the result?
options: It is both accurate and precise, so no improvement is needed
It is neither accurate nor precise, so the method is invalid
It is precise but not accurate, suggesting a systematic error
It is accurate but not precise, suggesting large random errors
questions.explanation: Results that are close together are precise, but a mean 4% above the accepted value is not accurate. A consistent offset like this points to a systematic error, such as a miscalibrated timer or ruler, which repeating the measurement would not remove.

questions.stem: When monochromatic light passes through a double slit, a pattern of bright and dark bands appears on a screen. What two wave effects produce it?
options: Polarisation at each slit and absorption where the two polarised beams overlap
Dispersion at each slit and diffraction where the two coloured beams overlap
Diffraction at each slit and interference where the diffracted waves overlap
Refraction at each slit and reflection where the two refracted waves overlap
questions.explanation: Each narrow slit diffracts the light so that it spreads out, and the two spreading waves overlap and interfere. Where they arrive in phase the interference is constructive (bright bands); where they arrive half a cycle apart it is destructive (dark bands).

questions.stem: Why must the slits in a double-slit experiment with light be very narrow?
options: Narrow slits polarise the light, which is needed before the two beams can interfere
Wide slits would let too much light through and damage the screen with too much heat
Diffraction is significant only when the slit width is close to light's tiny wavelength
Narrow slits make the light travel faster, so the bands are spaced further apart on the screen
questions.explanation: Light's wavelength is around 4 × 10⁻⁷ to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m. A slit much wider than this barely spreads the light, so the beams from the two slits would not overlap enough to interfere. Slits a fraction of a millimetre wide give noticeable diffraction.

questions.stem: At the second bright band out from the central maximum of a double-slit pattern, what is the path difference from the two slits?
options: 2λ
λ
questions.explanation: Bright bands occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, mλ, and the central maximum is m = 0. So the second bright band out has a path difference of 2λ. Path differences of λ/2 and 1.5λ give dark bands.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm reaches a point on a double-slit screen where the path difference is 1500 nm. What is seen there?
options: A dark band, because the path difference is 2.5 wavelengths
A bright band, because the path difference is 2.5 wavelengths
A bright band, because the path difference is a multiple of 300 nm
A dark band, because the path difference is more than a wavelength
questions.explanation: 1500/600 = 2.5, so the waves arrive half a cycle out of phase and cancel, giving a dark band (destructive interference). A bright band needs a whole number of wavelengths. Being more than a wavelength is not itself the deciding factor.

questions.stem: Which description matches the theoretical intensity graph for light through a double slit, plotted across the screen?
options: Two bright peaks only, one directly in line with each slit
Intensity that rises steadily from one edge of the screen to the other
Evenly spaced bright maxima of equal height, with zero intensity between
A single broad peak in the centre, with no other maxima on either side of it
questions.explanation: In the ideal double-slit model the maxima are evenly spaced and of equal brightness, separated by points of zero intensity where destructive interference is complete. Two peaks only, one behind each slit, is what a particle model of light would predict. In practice, diffraction at each slit makes the outer maxima fade.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a double slit with a slit separation of 0.20 mm. The screen is 2.0 m away. What is the spacing between adjacent bright bands?
options: 1.7 mm
6.0 mm
60 mm
questions.explanation: From d sin θ = mλ with small angles, the band spacing is y = λL/d = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.0/2.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻³ m. Slips with the powers of ten in nanometres or millimetres give answers 10 times too small or too large.

questions.stem: Bright bands from a double slit with separation 0.25 mm are 4.0 mm apart on a screen 1.6 m away. What is the wavelength of the light?
options: 625 nm
391 nm
questions.explanation: λ = dy/L = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 4.0 × 10⁻³/1.6 = 6.25 × 10⁻⁷ m, or 625 nm. Forgetting to divide by L gives 1000 nm, and dividing by L twice gives 391 nm. A slip converting millimetres gives 6250 nm.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, which change would make the bright bands further apart?
options: Making the light source much brighter
Moving the screen further from the slits
Moving the two slits further apart
Using blue light in place of red light
questions.explanation: The band spacing is y = λL/d, so it increases with the screen distance L and the wavelength λ, and decreases with slit separation d. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, so it gives closer bands. Brightness affects how bright the bands are, not where they fall.

questions.stem: A diffraction grating has 500 lines per millimetre. Light of wavelength 500 nm falls on it. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
questions.explanation: The line spacing is d = 1/500 mm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m, so sin θ = λ/d = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷/2.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.25, and θ ≈ 14.5°. Treating 0.25 as the angle in degrees gives 0.25°.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 650 nm falls on a grating with 500 lines per millimetre. What is the highest order of maximum that can be observed?
options: Fifth order
Third order
Fourth order
Second order
questions.explanation: With d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m, sin θ = mλ/d must be less than 1, so m < d/λ = 3.08. The highest observable order is m = 3. Rounding 3.08 up to 4 would need sin θ > 1, which is impossible.

questions.stem: Compared with a double slit of the same spacing, a diffraction grating gives maxima that are:
options: much sharper and brighter, at the same angles
broader and dimmer, at the very same angles
much sharper and brighter, at smaller angles
broader and dimmer, at larger angles
questions.explanation: The angles of the maxima depend only on d and λ through d sin θ = mλ, so they are unchanged. With many slits, waves cancel almost everywhere except very close to those angles, so the maxima are narrow, bright lines. This makes gratings useful for measuring wavelengths accurately.

questions.stem: White light passes through a diffraction grating. In each first-order spectrum, which colour is deviated least from the central maximum?
options: Green
Yellow
Violet
Red
questions.explanation: sin θ = mλ/d, so shorter wavelengths are deviated through smaller angles. Violet has the shortest visible wavelength, so it appears closest to the central white maximum, and red appears furthest out. This is the reverse of the order in a prism's spectrum.

questions.stem: What is the difference between linearly polarised light and unpolarised light?
options: In polarised light the electric field oscillates in one plane; in unpolarised light, in all planes
In polarised light the magnetic field is zero; in unpolarised light both fields are present
Polarised light travels in one direction only; unpolarised light spreads out in all directions
Polarised light has one frequency only; unpolarised light contains a mixture of frequencies
questions.explanation: Polarisation describes the plane of the electric field's oscillation. Light from a lamp or the Sun is unpolarised, with the electric field oscillating in all directions perpendicular to the beam. In linearly polarised light it oscillates in a single plane. A single frequency describes monochromatic light, not polarised light.

questions.stem: How does a polarising filter polarise unpolarised light?
options: It reflects the magnetic field back, so only the electric field gets through
It bends the light so that all its waves travel in exactly the same direction
It transmits only the electric field component along its transmission axis
It slows the light down until only one frequency is able to pass through
questions.explanation: A polariser lets through the component of the electric field parallel to its transmission axis and absorbs the perpendicular component. The light that emerges is polarised along that axis, and for unpolarised light half the intensity is transmitted.

questions.stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polarising filter. What intensity emerges?
options: I₀/4
I₀/2
I₀
questions.explanation: Unpolarised light has its electric field in all directions, and averaged over these the filter passes half the intensity. Malus's law applies to light that is already polarised, so it is not used for the first filter.

questions.stem: Polarised light of intensity 40 W m⁻² meets a polarising filter whose transmission axis is at 30° to the light's plane of polarisation. What intensity is transmitted?
options: 35 W m⁻²
20 W m⁻²
10 W m⁻²
30 W m⁻²
questions.explanation: By Malus's law, I = I_max cos² θ = 40 × cos² 30° = 40 × 0.75 = 30 W m⁻². Forgetting to square the cosine gives about 35 W m⁻², and using sin² 30° gives 10 W m⁻².

questions.stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through two polarisers whose transmission axes are at 60° to each other. What intensity emerges from the second?
options: I₀/8
I₀/4
I₀/2
3I₀/8
questions.explanation: The first polariser transmits I₀/2. The second transmits (I₀/2) cos² 60° = (I₀/2) × 0.25 = I₀/8. Forgetting the first halving gives I₀/4, and using sin² 60° gives 3I₀/8.

questions.stem: Two polarisers are crossed at 90°, so no light gets through. A third polariser is placed between them with its axis at 45° to each. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ enters. What emerges?
options: I₀/4
I₀/2
I₀/8
questions.explanation: After the first polariser the intensity is I₀/2; the middle one passes (I₀/2) cos² 45° = I₀/4; the last passes (I₀/4) cos² 45° = I₀/8. The middle polariser rotates the plane of polarisation, so some light now gets through crossed polarisers.

questions.stem: Why does polarisation provide evidence that light is a transverse wave?
options: Only transverse waves carry energy, so only they can pass through a filter
Only transverse waves oscillate across the beam in a direction a filter can select
Only transverse waves can travel through a vacuum without a medium to carry them
Only transverse waves can be reflected from a surface and refracted through glass
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave such as sound the oscillation is along the direction of travel, so there is no sideways direction for a filter to select. Light can be polarised, so its oscillations must be across the direction of travel. Reflection and refraction happen to longitudinal waves too.

questions.stem: How did the double-slit pattern count as evidence against a simple particle model of light?
options: Particles would make many bands, but they would be coloured instead of a single colour
Particles would make two bright bands behind the slits, not many bright and dark bands
Particles would spread out evenly over the whole screen, with no bright bands anywhere
Particles would bounce back from the slits, so no light would reach the screen at all
questions.explanation: A stream of particles travelling in straight lines through two slits would make two bright strips. The observed pattern of many bright and dark bands, including darkness where light from both slits arrives, is explained by waves interfering.

questions.stem: Which set of observations together provides the evidence for the wave model of light?
options: Interference, black-body radiation and line spectra
Refraction, the photoelectric effect and diffraction
Diffraction, interference and polarisation
Reflection, the photoelectric effect and polarisation
questions.explanation: Diffraction and interference are characteristic of waves, and polarisation shows those waves are transverse. The photoelectric effect and black-body radiation are evidence for the quantum (photon) model instead, and reflection and refraction can be explained by either model.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a gap. For which gap width will the light diffract most noticeably?
options: 1 mm
1 cm
1 m
1 µm
questions.explanation: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is close to the wavelength. A 1 µm gap is only twice the 500 nm wavelength, so the light spreads strongly. Gaps of a millimetre or more are thousands of times wider than the wavelength, so the light passes almost straight through.

questions.stem: The frequency of visible light is about 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is its wavelength in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/5 × 10¹⁴ = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m, or 600 nm, in the visible range. Multiplying c by f instead of dividing gives 1.5 × 10²³ m.

questions.stem: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has a longer wavelength than visible light?
options: Gamma rays
Infrared
Ultraviolet
X-rays
questions.explanation: In order of increasing wavelength the spectrum runs gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves and radio waves. Infrared therefore has longer wavelengths (and lower frequencies) than visible light, while the others have shorter wavelengths.

questions.stem: A mobile phone signal has a frequency of 2.0 GHz. What is its wavelength?
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/2.0 × 10⁹ = 0.15 m, in the microwave band. Dividing f by c gives 6.7 m, and treating 2.0 GHz as 2.0 × 10⁸ Hz gives 1.5 m.

questions.stem: A grating with line spacing 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m gives a first-order maximum 0.39 m from the centre of a screen 1.5 m away. The angle is too large for the small-angle approximation. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.explanation: The angle is large, so find it first: tan θ = 0.39/1.5, so θ ≈ 14.6° and sin θ ≈ 0.25. Then λ = d sin θ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.25 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. Using the small-angle form dy/L gives 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is noticeably out at this angle.
